title: Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention

concept.text: The innovation is manufacturable nuclear fuel that extracts substantially more usable energy from each loading while reliably retaining fission products during operation and specified accident conditions. High burnup describes greater energy extraction from the fuel; robust retention requires the fuel and its protective barriers to keep radioactive fission products contained throughout that extended service. The intended advance combines these capabilities in a qualified fuel system.

Conceptual synthesis: success has several distinct dimensions. A fuel particle can survive irradiation without establishing that every fission-product species remains contained. Good irradiation performance also does not establish accident performance, consistent manufacturing quality, or compatibility with an entire reactor core. The concept therefore concerns predictable performance within a defined operating and accident envelope; the supplied evidence does not establish absolute retention under every possible condition.

significance.text: The potentially transformative benefit is obtaining substantially more usable energy from a given quantity of uranium while maintaining reliable containment. DOE's 2009 report connects higher burnup with greater energy extraction and reduced used-fuel generation. If this capability were demonstrated in manufacturable fuel at full-core scale, longer fuel service could reduce refueling and fuel-handling requirements per unit of electricity generated.

Conditional synthesis: fewer fuel replacements and handling operations could improve operating flexibility and reactor economics, especially where access or maintenance is difficult. Those consequences depend on reactor design, qualification requirements, achievable service life, and manufacturing and operating costs. Strong particle-level performance alone does not establish a commercially transformative result.

Higher burnup does not by itself establish a particular reduction in total waste volume or fuel-cycle cost. The supplied article provides no whole-cycle accounting that supports a 90% reduction. Such a claim would require comparison of the complete fuel systems and their resulting waste streams, rather than inference from uranium utilization alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central capability to establish is a qualified, reproducibly manufactured fuel that combines very high energy extraction, predictable irradiation behavior, and fission-product retention during operation and specified accidents. DOE's reported program linked coated-particle manufacturing development with irradiation, post-irradiation examination, and subsequent accident testing. Its planned examination for degradation identifies an assessment requirement; it does not itself demonstrate a particular degradation mechanism or establish which qualification gaps remain today.

Engineering synthesis: the barriers include producing protective coatings consistently, establishing how their integrity and retention behavior change over extended irradiation, and measuring release of individual fission-product species under demanding conditions. A convincing advance must also show that the higher-burnup fuel remains compatible with the intended core's thermal, mechanical, and operating constraints. These are requirements for the proposed capability, not a verified inventory of unresolved deficiencies in present-day TRISO fuel.

Assessment synthesis: both 'very high burnup' and 'robust retention' need explicit reference points. Burnup must be compared with a relevant fuel- and reactor-specific baseline, while retention must specify the species measured, detection limits, exposure duration, and operating or accident conditions. Without those boundaries, a strong result in one experiment cannot establish the broader innovation.

current_state.text: On November 16, 2009, the U.S. Department of Energy reported that the AGR-1 experimental TRISO particle-fuel campaign at Idaho National Laboratory's Advanced Test Reactor had reached a maximum uranium burnup of 19% and an average of 16%. DOE reported no particle failures during irradiation. These are dated experimental achievements, not evidence that the broader proposed innovation has been completed.

The reported operational failure indicator was fission-product gas release indicative of coating failure. Accordingly, the absence of reported failures supports the irradiation-performance result within that monitoring framework; it does not establish zero release of every fission-product species. Particle survival and species-specific retention remain distinct measurements.

At publication, post-irradiation examination to assess coating degradation and subsequent higher-temperature accident testing were still planned. The article therefore does not establish the outcomes of those tests, universal accident retention, full-core compatibility, or performance at the proposed higher burnup. Planned testing should not be read as either a completed demonstration or evidence that the fuel failed.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review assessed the complete retained article body and reported no truncation or extraction problems. The available evidence nevertheless consists of this historical report, with no supplied freshness-search record or newer qualification results. It supports the 2009 achievement but cannot identify the strongest current result, current technical leadership, or the remaining qualification gaps as of November 2026. That limitation does not show that subsequent progress has or has not occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: define a reactor-specific current-practice baseline, then irradiate representative fuel manufactured by a reproducible process to substantially greater burnup. Report the distribution of achieved burnup and performance across the tested fuel, rather than relying on a single maximum. Repeat the demonstration across independent manufacturing batches and obtain independent assessment of the results. These are proposed criteria, not established qualification standards.
completion_criteria.label: Fuel substantially exceeds baseline burnup across independent manufacturing batches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed retention and integrity demonstration: measure species-specific fission-product release and mechanical integrity during irradiation, representative transients, and explicitly defined accident tests. State detection limits, test duration, temperatures, failure definitions, and the range of conditions examined. Independent replication and post-irradiation examination should support the interpretation. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, not literal retention under all conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Fission-product retention and integrity demonstrated within a defined test envelope

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: establish compatibility with the intended full core and show that the manufacturing process can consistently deliver the required fuel quality. Report fuel-cycle costs and waste streams against a defined comparator so that claims about refueling, handling, economics, or waste reduction can be evaluated on a common basis. Particle-level results alone would not satisfy these deployment criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Full-core compatibility and consistent fuel quality demonstrated with comparative accounting

completion_criteria.text: Optional research proposal: a 50% FIMA target could be considered as an ambitious objective, subject to fuel-specific feasibility assessment. FIMA expresses fissions per initial metal atom. The supplied source neither establishes the historical provenance of that target nor makes it a completion threshold; it should not substitute for a justified baseline and a complete performance envelope.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Fuel-specific feasibility assessment of the 50% FIMA target

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-06, 'Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure,' overlaps through irradiation durability, but focuses on reactor structures rather than the fuel and its fission-product barriers. NUC-11, 'Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants,' addresses the surrounding coolant environment and its material compatibility. NUC-08, 'Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling,' could complement fuel retention by controlling reactor conditions during accidents; successful fuel retention does not itself demonstrate shutdown or cooling.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-02, 'Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost,' could benefit from qualified fuel that reduces operating burdens, but fuel performance alone does not establish lower plant delivery costs. NUC-10, 'Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites,' has a direct potential connection through extended fuel service, while also requiring reliable performance from the rest of the power system. NUC-04, 'High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions,' could share demanding fuel-service requirements, but propulsion performance and mission readiness remain separate achievements.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-03, 'A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides,' concerns fuel-cycle processing and actinide consumption. Higher burnup in a fuel loading does not establish a closed cycle or consumption of most long-lived actinides. NUC-13, 'A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance,' addresses a separate system property that cannot be inferred from burnup or fission-product retention alone.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-12, 'Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis,' could provide complementary information about core behavior, but diagnosis does not establish fuel qualification. NUC-05, 'Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors,' concerns verification capabilities; the gas-release monitoring described for an irradiation experiment does not establish remote verification of operating reactors.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, 'A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant,' and NUC-07, 'Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle,' concern different energy-producing reactions and plant requirements. They share broad challenges of nuclear-system reliability but do not demonstrate the fission-fuel capability described here. NUC-09 retains its separate identity as the combination of very high fission-fuel burnup and robust fission-product retention.

change_log.reason: The article did not report the outcomes of those subsequent activities.

change_log.reason: The supplied source does not mention that target or establish it as a qualification threshold.

change_log.reason: These boundaries make the proposed capability assessable without treating finite demonstrations as universal proof.

unresolved_issues: The strongest current fuel-qualification result and remaining gaps as of November 2026 cannot be determined from the supplied historical article.
The fuel design, reactor-specific baseline, target burnup, and operating and accident envelopes for this innovation remain undefined.
The historical provenance and fuel-specific feasibility of a 50% FIMA objective remain unestablished.
Species-specific release measurements, detection limits, and subsequent examination and accident-test outcomes are not supplied.
Manufacturing reproducibility, full-core compatibility, whole-cycle costs, and waste-stream comparisons for the proposed capability remain to be demonstrated.

brief.title: Longer-lasting nuclear fuel that holds in radioactivity
possible: Nuclear plants could get substantially more energy from each fuel loading while keeping radioactive byproducts contained during normal operation and defined accident conditions. The fuel would last longer and could be manufactured consistently for use throughout a reactor.
why: More energy from the same uranium could mean fewer fuel replacements and less fuel handling per unit of electricity. For reactor operators, longer service could improve operating flexibility and economics, especially where maintenance or access is difficult.

sources.showed: Coated fuel particles achieved high energy extraction in a test reactor without gas releases indicating coating failure.
sources.quote: None of the fuel particles released an amount of fission product gases that would indicated failure of the three coating layers that surround each particle during the entire irradiation campaign.
sources.cited_for: This supports longer fuel service with protective coatings surviving reactor exposure.
sources.not_established: Gas monitoring did not establish containment of every radioactive byproduct or performance during accidents.

sources.showed: The team completed examinations of fuel after reactor exposure and high-temperature safety tests, studying radioactive releases and coating behavior.
sources.cited_for: This supports testing containment after reactor exposure and under accident conditions.
sources.not_established: Individual fuel tests do not establish consistent manufacturing quality or compatibility with an entire reactor core.

sources.showed: A small set of coated fuel samples retained key radioactive byproducts during accident heating tests. Hotter tests produced coating failures and greater releases.
sources.quote: no krypton was detected above the minimum detectable limit, and cesium releases were far below a single particle equivalent
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates containment during defined accident tests and shows that performance depends on temperature and the substance measured.
sources.not_established: The small sample does not establish containment across all fuel batches or accident conditions.

sources.showed: Preliminary heating results found little radioactive cesium release from samples operated at lower temperatures. A hotter-operated sample apparently suffered a protective coating failure.
sources.quote: For compacts with TAVA temperatures of less than 920°C, only small quantities of Cs were detected, indicating that no SiC layer had completely failed in any of the particles.
sources.cited_for: This supports assessing accident performance against the fuel's prior operating conditions.
sources.not_established: Preliminary results from a small sample do not establish reliable performance throughout the intended operating range.

shown: Idaho National Laboratory's coated fuel particles reached a maximum of 19% uranium consumption in a test reactor, without gas releases indicating coating failure.

Later work led by William F. Cureton tested small fuel samples at 1600°C without detecting krypton gas or cesium releases indicating coating failure. Hotter tests produced failures. Some other radioactive substances escaped even through intact coatings.
missing: Repeated batches must deliver substantially more energy than the intended reactor's usual fuel, with independent assessment.
Tests must establish how much of each radioactive byproduct escapes during extended operation and specified accidents.
Consistently manufactured fuel must work throughout the intended reactor core.
Complete fuel-system comparisons must establish costs, handling requirements and waste streams.

milestones.label: Repeated fuel batches substantially exceed usual energy extraction
milestones.explanation: Independent assessment would have to confirm substantially greater energy extraction across reproducibly manufactured batches against a reactor-specific baseline. This would establish repeatable performance beyond a single best result.

milestones.label: Containment and fuel integrity survive defined operating and accident tests
milestones.explanation: Replicated tests and examination afterward would have to establish coating integrity and releases of individual radioactive byproducts under defined conditions and detection limits. This would establish where containment is reliable.

milestones.label: Consistent fuel works throughout a reactor with measured practical benefits
milestones.explanation: Consistent manufacturing and compatibility with the intended core would have to be demonstrated, alongside comparative costs and waste streams. This would connect particle performance to practical reactor use.

milestones.label: An optional higher energy-extraction target proves feasible
milestones.explanation: A fuel-specific assessment would have to establish whether splitting 50% of the initial metal atoms is feasible. This would assess an optional stretch goal.

uncertain: The fuel design, reactor-specific comparison and intended operating and accident conditions remain undefined.
Reliable containment depends on which radioactive substances are measured, how sensitively and for how long.
The optional stretch target's feasibility remains an open question for each fuel design.

page.title: Qualified UCO TRISO compact fuel at 15–20% FIMA
page.definition: UCO TRISO fuel consists of uranium oxide–carbide kernels within carbon and silicon-carbide coatings, embedded in graphite compacts. It is qualified for a named reactor at 15–20% FIMA—15–20% of initial heavy-metal atoms fissioned—with radioactive releases within that reactor's operating and accident limits.

goal.need: The AGR programme targets a 15–20% FIMA fuel envelope. DOE's historical comparison below illustrates the difference from light-water-reactor fuel in uranium utilization. More fissions per initial fuel mass provide more fission energy; qualification must also establish retention during operation and accidents. These figures do not quantify whole-system waste reduction.

figures.caption: DOE's uranium-burnup comparison published on 16 November 2009.
figures.note: A historical comparison, not a statement of present licensing limits; the TRISO values were proposed operating examples.

completion.title: CNSC confirms UCO TRISO compact fuel is qualified for reactor use at 15–20% FIMA.
completion.criterion: Obtain Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission staff confirmation that the specified UCO TRISO compact fuel design is within a named reactor's licensing basis and qualified for use. Its documented qualification envelope must include a specified maximum burnup within the DOE AGR target range of 15–20% FIMA, with manufacturing specifications, qualification results and the reactor safety case supporting operation and specified accidents.
completion.set_by: Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, REGDOC-2.4.5, section 6, sets the qualification-confirmation test for the Canadian licensing route. DOE AGR's published design envelope supplies the burnup range.
completion.threshold_quote: the design is within the licensing basis and is qualified for use:
completion.basis: CNSC explicitly requires qualification confirmation before loading a new fuel design. This provides an application-specific acceptance test covering the manufactured fuel and its reactor safety case. The numerical burnup range comes from DOE's programme rather than a universal regulatory burnup limit. This completion route applies to Canadian licensing.

milestones.title: Laboratory UCO TRISO fuel meets the AGR-1 product specification, with documented minor exceptions.
milestones.criterion: Produce baseline and variant UCO TRISO test articles meeting AGR-1 product specifications; the published success criterion permits minor exceptions addressed by nonconformance reports. AGR-1 subsequently irradiated 72 compacts in six capsules. Its final as-run report records kernel fabrication and particle coating in accordance with the AGR-1 specification.
milestones.set_by: DOE AGR programme, The AGR-1 Irradiation – Objectives, Success Criteria and Risk Management, section 4.2.2(1). This criterion concerns laboratory-scale AGR-1 compact fuel.
milestones.threshold_quote: Production of baseline and variant fuel test articles meeting AGR-1 specification requirements

milestones.title: UCO TRISO fuel reaches ≥15% FIMA with krypton-85m R/B ≤4 × 10⁻⁶ and ≤5 particle failures.
milestones.criterion: Operate at least one fuel capsule to ≥15% FIMA with krypton-85m release-rate/birth-rate ratio ≤4.0 × 10⁻⁶ and ≤5 particle failures indicated by gross fission-product monitor spikes. AGR-1 irradiated 72 compacts for 620 effective full-power days, ending on 6 November 2009: compact burnups were 11.3–19.6% FIMA and no particle failures were detected. Capsule-average burnups reached 18.6% FIMA.
milestones.set_by: DOE AGR programme, The AGR-1 Irradiation – Objectives, Success Criteria and Risk Management, section 4.2.2(4). The published criterion concerns instrumented AGR-1 fuel capsules.
milestones.threshold_quote: Operation of one or more capsules to burnup ≥ 15% FIMA

milestones.title: Engineering-scale UCO TRISO compacts have ≤10⁻⁴ defective SiC coatings at 95% confidence.
milestones.criterion: Manufacture engineering-scale compacts meeting SPC-1352 Table 4: defective silicon-carbide coating fraction ≤1.0 × 10⁻⁴, exposed-kernel fraction ≤5.0 × 10⁻⁵ and mean dispersed-uranium fraction ≤1.0 × 10⁻⁵, assessed at 95% confidence. In the June 2020 fabrication report, ORNL's confirmatory SiC upper bounds were 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ (348,000 particles) and 5.7 × 10⁻⁵ (137,400). The 40% particle-packing-fraction compacts exceeded the exposed-kernel limit.
milestones.set_by: DOE AGR programme and Idaho National Laboratory, AGR-5/6/7 Fuel Specification, SPC-1352 Revision 8, Table 4 and Part 2. Numerical thresholds appear in the table. These specifications concern AGR-5/6/7 experimental compacts.

milestones.title: Irradiated UCO TRISO fuel has ≤2 × 10⁻⁴ complete failures at 1600°C for 300 h, at 95% confidence.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate complete-TRISO failure fraction ≤2 × 10⁻⁴ at 95% confidence after nominal 300 h holds at 1600°C in helium; ≥15,000 particles are needed with zero failures. Earlier AGR-1/2 tests found zero complete failures among 45,804 particles. A 2025 technical report, not peer reviewed, tested three AGR-5/6/7 compacts at 1600°C for about 300 h, finding no detectable krypton and cesium release below one particle equivalent. One compact at 1800°C had evidence of one complete failure and two SiC failures. In-pile silver loss occurred.
milestones.set_by: DOE AGR programme, AGR-5/6/7 Post-Irradiation Examination Plan, sections 2.15.1.1–2.15.1.3. The ≤2 × 10⁻⁴ programme target provides margin below the cited historical accident-design criterion of ≤6 × 10⁻⁴.
milestones.threshold_quote: A failure fraction of ≤2E-4 can be demonstrated by testing 15,000 particles if zero failures are observed.

milestones.title: UCO TRISO fuel meets every design requirement and limit for its intended reactor.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate that the manufactured UCO TRISO fuel meets all design requirements and associated limits for the named reactor's operating and accident envelope, using testing, analysis and applicable operating experience. Include radionuclide retention, coolability and safe shutdown. DOE's April 2026 strategy describes AGR-5/6/7 post-irradiation examination and accident testing as ongoing; it does not establish this reactor-specific result.
milestones.set_by: Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, REGDOC-2.4.5, sections 2, 5.1 and 5.2. This is the technical qualification requirement preceding confirmation under section 6 for the Canadian licensing route.
milestones.threshold_quote: the design meets all of the requirements and the associated limits.

not_found: Searches found no reactor-specific qualification confirmation for UCO TRISO compact fuel at 15–20% FIMA.
Searches of DOE, NRC and IAEA material found no fuel-qualification criterion of 50% FIMA.
NRC's final NUREG-2246 and its 2020 safety evaluation of the EPRI TRISO topical report could not be retrieved.
